analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare for seniors and disabled people.
analysis.headline: The bill gained 52 cosponsors but never received a committee hearing or vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare currently excludes most dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids, so older Americans pay out of pocket or go without. This bill would have added coverage for cleanings, fillings, dentures, eye exams, glasses, contact lenses, hearing exams, and hearing aids, with limits like one hearing aid per ear every four years and a payment schedule that starts at zero percent of cost and phases up to 80 percent over eight years.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of people on Medicare, who today either pay fully out of pocket for dental care, glasses, and hearing aids or go without them. Untreated dental disease and hearing loss are linked to pain, infections, and social isolation; the bill would have covered routine cleanings and exams, fillings, root canals, extractions, emergency dental care, dentures once every five years, annual eye exams, eyeglasses and contact lenses, and hearing aids.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Covers routine dental cleanings and exams twice a year, plus fillings, crowns, root canals, extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures once every five years [S2].
Covers routine eye exams once a year, eyeglass lenses, frames, contact lenses up to $200 per two years, and low vision devices [S2].
Covers routine hearing exams and hearing aids, limited to one hearing aid per ear every four years, and repeals the Medicare exclusion that currently bans payment for hearing aids [S3].

Medicare would pay 0 percent of the cost in the first year, ramping up 10 percentage points a year to 80 percent from the eighth year onward, with the Secretary of Health and Human Services able to add reasonable limits or prior authorization [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Medicare program, which would absorb new spending with no dedicated funding source in the bill. Providers would receive reduced payments during the eight-year phase-in, and beneficiaries would still owe coinsurance on the covered amount.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no financing provision, so the new benefits would be an unfunded addition to Medicare spending, drawing on payroll tax and general revenue that already face long-term solvency pressure [S3].

In the first year Medicare would pay providers 0 percent of the payment amount for these services, ramping to only 80 percent by the eighth year, which could leave some dentists, audiologists, and optical suppliers unwilling to participate early on [S3].

The bill gives the Health and Human Services Secretary broad authority to impose additional limits and prior authorization on the new benefits, so the actual scope of coverage would depend on administrative choices after passage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial: Medicare is the only large health program that excludes dental, vision, and hearing care outright, and gaps in these services fall hardest on lower-income seniors, who skip cleanings, glasses, and hearing aids they cannot afford. The cost is real but ordinary for a benefit expansion, and the bill at least controlled it through frequency limits and a long payment phase-in. The honest weakness is that it was never scored or funded, so taxpayers would be paying for an expansion whose financing was left to a later Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a Health subcommittee in February 2019 and never moved again; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 27, 2019 [S1].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
It was then referred to the Health Subcommittee, the standard first stop for Medicare bills, where it sat [S5].
Fifty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but no action of any kind followed the referrals [S4].
The last recorded action was the March 1, 2019 subcommittee referral; nothing occurred for the remaining 22 months of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody moved the bill, so the status quo held: dental, vision, and hearing device industries kept selling to seniors at retail prices, Medicare Advantage insurers kept marketing dental and vision add-ons as perks, and Medicare beneficiaries kept paying out of pocket or going without.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industries selling dental, vision, and hearing care out of pocket

sides.party_line_note: All 52 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.note: Medicare would become a new payer for cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures, bringing in patients who currently skip care because they cannot pay. Payments phase in slowly, starting at 0 percent.
The bill repeals Medicare's long-standing exclusion on hearing aids, creating coverage for devices that often cost thousands of dollars per ear. The one-per-ear-every-four-years limit caps volume.
Annual eye exams, lenses, frames, and contact lens allowances would be covered, opening a large insured market. Payment also phases in from 0 to 80 percent over eight years.

Many private Medicare Advantage plans offer limited dental, vision, and hearing benefits as their main selling point. Universal coverage through original Medicare would erase that marketing advantage.
